prompt.context: Your client Pharmaco is a retail pharmacy (think CVS), and is considering changing their prescription from monthly pickup to every three months.
prompt.question: What are the major considerations to this change?

exhibits.title: Average Adherence Percentage Over Three Years
exhibits.shows: A chart comparing prescription adherence rates over time between the monthly pickup option and the 3-month pickup option

exhibits.title: Price Per Fill by Customer Segment
exhibits.shows: A table showing price per fill for 1-month and 3-month options across three customer segments (A, B, C)

framework: 1. Profit Considerations: effect on prescription revenue, prescription adherence, effect on other in-store sales, cost savings
2. Market Considerations: competitor reaction / competitive advantage, regulatory environment
3. Company Considerations: brand impact, customer loyalty (some may prefer 1-month option)

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 1, would you recommend moving to 3 months? What else would you need to think about?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that 3-month adherence (60%) is higher than monthly adherence (50%), which is a positive signal for revenue and patient outcomes. Beyond adherence, strong answers will raise: (1) effect on overall store sales because fewer pharmacy visits means fewer impulse/ancillary purchases; (2) risks with addictive or high-loss-risk drugs; (3) insurance regulation compatibility; (4) potential labor/workload reduction for pharmacists due to lower traffic.

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 2, does it make sense to go with 1 month or 3 month? What are some risks to segmenting customers or providing a 3-month option altogether?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute and compare annual revenue per customer for each segment under both options. Segment A favors 3-month; Segment B is revenue-neutral; Segment C is worse under 3-month. Segmenting is optimal, but even without segmentation the aggregate gain from A outweighs the loss from C. Improved adherence in the 3-month option makes the case even stronger over the long run.

math.setup: Annual revenue = fills per year x price per fill. Monthly: 12 fills/year. 3-Month: 4 fills/year.
steps: Segment A Monthly: 12 x $3 = $36 | 3-Month: 4 x $12 = $48 → gain of $12
Segment B Monthly: 12 x $12.50 = $150 | 3-Month: 4 x $37.50 = $150 → no change
Segment C Monthly: 12 x $5 = $60 | 3-Month: 4 x $13 = $52 → loss of $8
Net effect (A+B+C) if all switch: +$12 + $0 - $8 = +$4 net gain per customer
math.answer: Segment A benefits materially from 3-month; Segment B is indifferent; Segment C declines. Segmenting and offering 3-month only to A and B is optimal. Even without segmentation, net revenue is positive. Higher adherence in 3-month further strengthens the case.

recommendation: Pharmaco should switch to the 3-month option, preferably by segmenting customers: offer 3-month to Segment A and B while keeping Segment C on the 1-month option
Even without segmentation the aggregate prescription revenue impact is positive, and higher adherence under the 3-month option makes it more profitable over the long run
risks: Loss from other in-store sales because patients visit the pharmacy fewer times per year under the 3-month option
The 3-month option may conflict with insurance regulations
Pharmaco may lose customers who prefer the 1-month option and can obtain it from competitors
next_steps: Estimate loss from other (non-prescription) sales to confirm it does not overshadow the gain in prescription revenue
Verify that the 3-month option is compatible with insurance regulations
Run a pilot program with specific drug categories before full rollout
